sections.heading: Cronus strikes
sections.translation:
Gaia, the goddess Earth, hid her son Cronus in ambush.
She put a jagged-toothed sickle in his hands
and told him the whole plan.

Then mighty Uranus, the god Sky, came bringing night.
Longing to make love, he spread himself
all over Earth. From his hiding place,
his son reached out with his left hand;
with his right he gripped the huge, long, jagged sickle
and swiftly sliced off his own father’s genitals,
flinging them behind him.

But they did not leave his hand without a result.
Earth caught every drop of blood that scattered,
and as the years rolled round, she gave birth
to the powerful Erinyes, spirits of vengeance,
and the great Giants, gleaming in armor,
long spears in their hands,
and the Meliae, ash-tree spirits,
whom people across the boundless earth call by that name.
sections.summary: Cronus cuts off his father Sky’s genitals. The blood falls on Earth, who later gives birth to spirits of vengeance, Giants, and ash-tree spirits.

cards.label: Gaia
cards.general: Earth herself, imagined as a goddess.
cards.here: She hides Cronus, gives him the weapon, and receives Sky’s blood.

cards.label: Cronus
cards.general: A divine son of Earth and Sky.
cards.here: He attacks his father from a hiding place.

cards.label: Uranus
cards.general: Sky himself, imagined as a god; his Greek name is Ouranos.
cards.here: He spreads over Earth and is attacked by his son.

cards.label: Sickle
cards.general: A curved blade usually used to cut crops.
cards.here: Cronus uses a huge version with a jagged cutting edge.

cards.label: Genitals
cards.general: The external sexual organs.
cards.here: Cronus cuts off his father’s genitals and throws them behind him.

cards.label: Erinyes
cards.general: Goddesses of vengeance, also called the Furies.
cards.here: Earth gives birth to them after receiving Sky’s blood.

cards.label: Giants
cards.general: A race of powerful beings born from Earth.
cards.here: They appear as warriors with shining armor and long spears.

cards.label: Meliae
cards.general: Nymphs, or female nature spirits, associated with ash trees.
cards.here: They too are born from Earth after Sky’s blood falls on her.

sections.heading: Aphrodite from the foam
sections.translation:
Once Cronus had cut off the genitals
with adamant—a substance nothing could break—
and thrown them from the land into the surging sea,
they drifted over the water for a long time.
White foam rose around the immortal flesh,
and in that foam a girl grew.

First she drew near holy Cythera, an island;
then she reached Cyprus, surrounded by the sea.
Out stepped a beautiful goddess, worthy of reverence,
and grass grew beneath her slender feet.

Gods and humans call her Aphrodite, the goddess of love,
because she grew in foam—the Greek word is aphros.
They call her Cytherea because she came to Cythera,
and Cyprus-born because she was born on wave-washed Cyprus,
and “Genital-loving” because she appeared from genitals.

Eros, the god Love, went with her,
and beautiful Himeros, the god Desire, followed,
from the moment of her birth
as she went to join the company of gods.

From the beginning, this has been her honor,
the share assigned to her among humans and immortal gods:
young women’s intimate whispers, smiles and deceptions,
sweet pleasure, lovemaking, and tenderness.
sections.summary: Aphrodite grows in sea foam around Sky’s severed genitals. Love and Desire accompany her, and she receives power over attraction, pleasure, and lovemaking.

cards.label: Adamant
cards.general: A legendary substance imagined as extraordinarily hard.
cards.here: It is the material of Cronus’s cutting blade.

cards.label: Aphrodite
cards.general: The goddess of love, sexual attraction, and pleasure.
cards.here: She grows in sea foam and steps ashore on Cyprus.

cards.label: Aphros
cards.general: The Greek word for foam.
cards.here: Hesiod uses its sound to explain Aphrodite’s name.

cards.label: Cythera / Cytherea
cards.general: Cythera is an island south of mainland Greece; Cytherea means “goddess of Cythera.”
cards.here: Aphrodite approaches this holy island before reaching Cyprus.

cards.label: Cyprus / Cyprus-born
cards.general: Cyprus is an island in the eastern Mediterranean.
cards.here: Hesiod connects Aphrodite’s title “Cyprus-born” with her birth and arrival there.

cards.label: Genital-loving
cards.general: A startling divine nickname built around a Greek word for genitals.
cards.here: Hesiod connects the nickname with the body parts from which Aphrodite appeared.

cards.label: Eros
cards.general: Love, especially sexual attraction, imagined as a god.
cards.here: He accompanies Aphrodite from her birth.

cards.label: Himeros
cards.general: Longing or desire, imagined as a god.
cards.here: He follows Aphrodite as she joins the gods.

sections.heading: The Titans get their name
sections.translation:
Their father, mighty Sky, called the children
he himself had fathered “Titans,” in reproach.
He said they had strained too far in their recklessness,
committing a terrible deed—
and that punishment for it would come later.
sections.summary: Sky calls his children Titans, blaming their reckless act and warning that they will pay for it.

cards.label: Titans
cards.general: A generation of gods born from Earth and Sky, including Cronus.
cards.here: Sky uses the name as an accusation. Hesiod links its sound with Greek words for straining and punishment.

cards.label: Reproach
cards.general: Words expressing blame or strong disapproval.
cards.here: Sky gives his children their name while condemning what they have done.

sections.heading: Night’s many children
sections.translation:
Night gave birth to hateful Moros, the doom awaiting us,
to black Ker, a spirit of death, and to Thanatos, Death himself.
She bore Hypnos, Sleep, and the whole tribe of Dreams.
The dark goddess Night bore them without sleeping with anyone.

Then she bore Momus, Blame, and Oizys, painful Misery,
and the Hesperides, maidens who tend the beautiful golden apples
and the trees that bear them,
beyond famous Oceanus, the river circling the world.

She also bore the Fates and the Keres, merciless avengers—
Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos,
who give mortals their share of good and bad at birth.
They pursue the wrongdoing of humans and gods,
and these goddesses never let their terrible anger rest
until they make whoever has done wrong pay dearly.

Deadly Night also bore Nemesis, the goddess of payback,
a source of suffering for mortals.
After her she bore Apate, Deceit, and Philotes, Intimacy,
and destructive Old Age,
and Eris, fierce-hearted Strife.
sections.summary: Night gives birth on her own to many divine beings, including Death, Sleep, Dreams, the Fates, and Strife.

cards.label: Night
cards.general: Night herself, imagined as a goddess; her Greek name is Nyx.
cards.here: She produces these children without a sexual partner.

cards.label: Moros
cards.general: Doom or an unavoidable fate, imagined as a divine being.
cards.here: He is Night’s first child named in this list.

cards.label: Ker / Keres
cards.general: Ker is a spirit of death or fatal doom; Keres is the plural.
cards.here: A single black Ker appears first; later the Keres appear as merciless avengers.

cards.label: Thanatos
cards.general: Death himself, imagined as a god.
cards.here: He is a child of Night and a brother of Sleep.

cards.label: Hypnos
cards.general: Sleep himself, imagined as a god.
cards.here: Night bears him alongside Death and the Dreams.

cards.label: Dreams
cards.general: Dreams imagined as a family of divine beings.
cards.here: Night gives birth to their whole tribe.

cards.label: Momus
cards.general: Blame or fault-finding, imagined as a god.
cards.here: He is one of Night’s children.

cards.label: Oizys
cards.general: Misery or distress, imagined as a goddess.
cards.here: Hesiod describes her as painful.

cards.label: Hesperides
cards.general: Divine maidens associated with the evening and the far west.
cards.here: They tend golden apples and the trees that grow them.

cards.label: Oceanus
cards.general: The great river believed to circle the world, also imagined as a god.
cards.here: The Hesperides care for their trees beyond it.

cards.label: Fates
cards.general: Goddesses who assign each person’s lot in life; their Greek name is Moirai.
cards.here: They give people good and bad at birth and appear alongside powers that punish wrongdoing.

cards.label: Clotho
cards.general: One of the three named Fates; her name means “Spinner.”
cards.here: She is named with Lachesis and Atropos among those who assign people their lot.

cards.label: Lachesis
cards.general: One of the three named Fates; her name means “Allotter.”
cards.here: She helps assign the good and bad people receive in life.

cards.label: Atropos
cards.general: One of the three named Fates; her name means “Unturning” or “Unchangeable.”
cards.here: She appears with Clotho and Lachesis.

cards.label: Nemesis
cards.general: A goddess of resentment and deserved payback for wrongdoing.
cards.here: Night bears her as a source of suffering for mortals.

cards.label: Apate
cards.general: Deceit imagined as a goddess.
cards.here: She is born after Nemesis.

cards.label: Philotes
cards.general: Affection or intimacy, including sexual intimacy, imagined as a goddess.
cards.here: She is another child of Night.

cards.label: Old Age
cards.general: Old age imagined as a divine being, called Geras in Greek.
cards.here: Hesiod calls it destructive.

cards.label: Eris
cards.general: Strife or conflict imagined as a goddess.
cards.here: She is Night’s fierce-hearted child.

uncertainties: At line 200, “Genital-loving” follows the supplied Greek spelling and its explicit explanation. The nickname also echoes Aphrodite’s familiar title “smile-loving”; the exact relationship between the two forms is debated.
In lines 217–222, the wording blends the Fates and the Keres. Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos are the Fates, but it is unclear exactly which group each following description is meant to cover.
